title: The Thief and the Guru's House (ಕನ್ನಡ)
summary: One moonless midnight, a professional housebreaker named Kalla entered the quiet village. Seeking easy plunder, he slipped over the garde... [KN]
keywords: the thief and the guru's house
full_text:
One moonless midnight, a professional housebreaker named Kalla entered the quiet village. Seeking easy plunder, he slipped over the garden wall of Guru Paramartha's ashram and crept toward the open window of the central hall.

The ashram was quiet. The five disciples were snoring in a heap on the veranda, while Guru Paramartha lay awake upon his cot, suffering from a mild touch of indigestion brought on by eating unboiled lentils.

Hearing the soft scraping of the thief's iron jemmy against the wooden shutter, the Guru sat up and called out in a dignified, scholarly voice: 'Who knocks at the portal of philosophy at this unseasonable hour? Is it a seeker of divine truth, or a pilgrim with an offering of ghee?'

The thief, surprised by this gentle reception, realized he was dealing with the famous foolish Guru. Stepping boldly through the window, the thief whispered: 'I am a humble nocturnal seeker, Master! I have come to relieve you of your heavy worldly burdens!'

The Guru nodded with profound approval: 'Ah! You speak with allegorical wisdom, friend! The worldly possessions of this ashram are indeed a burden upon our spiritual contemplation. What burdens do you seek to remove?'

The thief pointed to the brass oil lamps, the silver prayer bells, and the heavy copper cooking cauldrons: 'Those heavy brass and copper vessels, Master! They produce terrible karmic weight!'

'Take them, honest seeker!' proclaimed the Guru. 'Take them, and let our souls be light!'

The thief stuffed the valuable vessels into his canvas sack. Looking around, his eyes fell upon a heavy wooden iron-bound chest in the corner, wherein the Guru stored his silver coins and festival robes.

The thief tried to lift the chest, but it was too heavy for one man: 'Master, this chest is exceptionally heavy with sin! I cannot carry it over the wall alone!'

Guru Paramartha immediately called out: 'Matti! Madayan! Peedan! Wake up, lazy boys! A noble seeker needs assistance in carrying away our worldly sins!'

The five disciples stumbled into the room, rubbing their sleepy eyes.

'What is our duty, Master?' asked Matti.

The Guru instructed: 'Help this honest brother lift this heavy chest upon his shoulders, and escort him politely to the garden gate!'

The five disciples eagerly lifted the heavy iron chest and hoisted it onto the thief's back. Asadan held the thief's torch; Peedan opened the gate, and Mudan bowed low, saying: 'Go in peace, brother, and do not stumble over the stones!'

The delighted thief bowed with a chuckle: 'May your wisdom spread through all the worlds, O Guru!' and vanished into the darkness with the ashram's entire fortune.

Next morning, the village headman arrived to pay respects. Finding the ashram bare of lamps, pots, and the treasure chest, the headman was appalled: 'Master, you have been robbed! Where are your valuables?'

Guru Paramartha smiled with serene, elevated detachment: 'We were not robbed, headman! A nocturnal philosopher visited us and relieved us of all our material entanglements! My disciples carried the chest to the gate with their own hands!'

The headman slapped his forehead in despair: 'You old fool, you gave your life savings to a common highway burglar!'

The Guru turned to his disciples and shook his head with pity: 'Observe, my children, how worldly men misunderstand the higher economics of spiritual liberation!'
moral: A pedantic host who reasons with a robber loses his goods and thanks the thief for his trouble. [KN]
